\chapter{The Vowels That Start a Word}
\label{ch:ka-svaragalu}
\hlchaptermodality{78}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write the six independent vowels a Kannada word can begin with, name the words I already say that start on them, and say how many times my pen leaves the page for each.}

From cold: name the six vowel letters, sort them by how many pen lifts each one takes, name the word you already say that opens on each, and say what this book does about a character whose stroke order nobody has published.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ā]{\kn{ಆ} — the same shape, held longer}

\label{lesson:KA-S155-letter-aa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಅ} — what sound does it carry, and how many times does your pen leave the page for it?

Today's character is that one with one more piece.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಆ}} — \emph{ā}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — the shape \emph{ā} takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside one.

Set it beside the one you already write:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{short} & \textbf{long} \\
\midrule
\kn{ಅ} \emph{a} & \kn{ಆ} \emph{ā} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The two are built from the same four parts} — a compact left loop, a broad lower bowl, a rounded right loop, an inward horizontal bar — and the hand tells them apart by where it stops rather than by what it draws. More on that in the writing section.

You already say these:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಆರು}} \emph{āru} — six
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಆಕಾಶ}} \emph{ākāśa} — sky
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಆಮೇಲೆ}} \emph{āmēle} — afterwards
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಆ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} turn clockwise around the compact left loop
  \item \textbf{2.} without lifting, sweep around the broad lower bowl and finish at the upper right
  \item \textbf{3.} lift, then turn clockwise around the rounded right loop
  \item \textbf{4.} without lifting, return left along the inward horizontal bar
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 1.} The left loop flows through the broad lower bowl; after one lift, the right loop returns left along the inner bar.

\kn{ಅ} runs all four movements without the pen leaving the page. \kn{ಆ} stops once, at the upper right, before the last two. \textbf{Same four parts, one lift apart} — and that lift is the thing to feel for, because it is what your hand will remember when your eye is still deciding.

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — Kannada handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Gopala Krishna A, 'Kannada-alphabet-aa.gif', 35 frames, Wikimedia Commons, 25 May 2016, CC BY-SA 4.0.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two words and say which opens on \kn{ಅ} and which on \kn{ಆ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಅಥವಾ}  ·  \kn{ಆರು}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಆ} three times, counting the one lift as you go
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a} and \emph{ā}, holding the second one twice as long
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಆ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ā}}.) How many times does your pen leave the page? (\textbf{Once} — and for \kn{ಅ}, not at all.) Which four parts do the two of them share?
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[e]{\kn{ಎ} — one run of the pen, four movements}

\label{lesson:KA-S156-letter-e}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಆ} — what sound, and how many lifts?

Count to ten. Two of those numbers open on today's character.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಎ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಎ}} — \emph{e}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — the shape \emph{e} takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside one.

You already say these:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಎರಡು}} \emph{eraḍu} — two
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಎಂಟು}} \emph{eṇṭu} — eight
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಎಲ್ಲಿ}} \emph{elli} — where
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಎಲೆ}} \emph{ele} — leaf
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Two of the first ten numbers begin with it}, which is why it is worth a page even though it looks like a shape you could pick up by copying. A character you meet while counting is one you will meet every day.

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಎ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} turn clockwise around the compact left loop
  \item \textbf{2.} without lifting, sweep through the joined lower-left curve
  \item \textbf{3.} without lifting, turn around the rounded lower-right bowl and climb its right side
  \item \textbf{4.} without lifting, carry the tall outer arch over and finish to the left
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 0.} The compact left loop flows through both lower curves, climbs the right side, and finishes left along the tall outer arch — one continuous run from first movement to last.

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — Kannada handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Gopala Krishna A, 'Kannada-alphabet-ae.gif', 30 frames, Wikimedia Commons, 25 May 2016, CC BY-SA 4.0.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two numbers and find \kn{ಎ} at the front of each
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಎರಡು}  ·  \kn{ಎಂಟು}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಎ} three times without letting the pen leave the page
  \item \emph{Say it:} which of \kn{ಆ} and \kn{ಎ} needs a lift and which does not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಎ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{e}}.) Which two numbers under ten open on it? (\textbf{\kn{ಎರಡು}} and \textbf{\kn{ಎಂಟು}}.) How many times does your pen leave the page? (\textbf{Not at all}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ē]{\kn{ಏ} — the end of the first question you learned to ask}

\label{lesson:KA-S157-letter-ee}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಎ} — what sound, and how many lifts?

Ask somebody their name in Kannada. The last word of that question opens on today's character.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಏ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಏ}} — \emph{ē}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — the shape \emph{ē} takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside one.

You already say these:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಏನು}} \emph{ēnu} — what?
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಏಳು}} \emph{ēḷu} — seven
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಏಕೆಂದರೆ}} \emph{ēkendare} — because
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\kn{ಏನು} closes the first question this book taught you} — \kn{ನಿಮ್ಮ} \kn{ಹೆಸರು} \kn{ಏನು}?, back in chapter two. Until now you could ask it out loud without being able to write its last piece.

Set it beside the one from the page before:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{short} & \textbf{long} \\
\midrule
\kn{ಎ} \emph{e} & \kn{ಏ} \emph{ē} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The long one carries \textbf{a small loop above} the body the short one ends with. Your pen builds the same lower body, then adds that loop separately.

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಏ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} turn clockwise around the compact left loop
  \item \textbf{2.} without lifting, sweep through the joined lower curves and climb the right side
  \item \textbf{3.} without lifting, carry the tall outer arch over and finish at the upper left
  \item \textbf{4.} lift, then draw the small upper loop from left to right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 1.} Write the joined lower body and tall arch in one run, then lift once for the small upper loop.

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — Kannada handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Gopala Krishna A, 'Kannada-alphabet-aee.gif', 31 frames, Wikimedia Commons, 25 May 2016, CC BY-SA 4.0.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two and say which is the short vowel and which the long
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಎರಡು}  ·  \kn{ಏಳು}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಏ} three times, stopping after the arch before the upper loop
  \item \emph{Say it:} the question \kn{ನಿಮ್ಮ} \kn{ಹೆಸರು} \kn{ಏನು}? and point at \kn{ಏ} as you say it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಏ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ē}}.) What does the lift come before? (\textbf{The small upper loop}.) Which number under ten opens on it? (\textbf{\kn{ಏಳು}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[o]{\kn{ಒ} — the letter the counting starts on}

\label{lesson:KA-S158-letter-o}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಏ} — what sound, and what comes after the lift?

Now say the number one. Today's character is where it starts.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಒ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಒ}} — \emph{o}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — the shape \emph{o} takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside one.

You already say these:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಒಂದು}} \emph{ondu} — one
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತು}} \emph{ombattu} — nine
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಒಳ್ಳೆಯ}} \emph{oḷḷeya} — good
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The first number you ever counted in this language opens on it}, and so does nine. A character that turns up twice inside one to ten is one you will meet every day.

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಒ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} turn counterclockwise around the compact upper-left loop
  \item \textbf{2.} without lifting, descend through the curved middle into the lower-left bowl
  \item \textbf{3.} without lifting, sweep through the join and around the lower-right bowl
  \item \textbf{4.} without lifting, climb the right side and curl left at the open terminal
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 0.} The upper loop, the curved descent, both lower bowls and the open terminal come out of one uninterrupted run.

\textbf{Notice the first movement goes counterclockwise.} \kn{ಆ}, \kn{ಎ} and \kn{ಏ} all opened with a clockwise turn around their left loop; this one turns the other way. It is the kind of difference the eye slides over and the hand does not.

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — Kannada handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Gopala Krishna A, 'Kannada-alphabet-o.gif', 30 frames, Wikimedia Commons, 25 May 2016, CC BY-SA 4.0.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two numbers and find \kn{ಒ} at the front of each
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಒಂದು}  ·  \kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತು}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಒ} three times, starting counterclockwise each time
  \item \emph{Say it:} which way the pen turns first for \kn{ಒ}, and which way for \kn{ಏ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಒ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{o}}.) Which number opens on it? (\textbf{\kn{ಒಂದು}} — and \textbf{\kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತು}}.) Which direction does the first turn go? (\textbf{Counterclockwise}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ai]{\kn{ಐ} — a vowel your mouth moves through}

\label{lesson:KA-S159-letter-ai}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಒ} — what sound, and which way does the first turn go?

Say the number five, slowly. Listen to the opening.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಐ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಐ}} — \emph{ai}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — the shape \emph{ai} takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside one.

You already say these:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಐದು}} \emph{aidu} — five
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಐದನೆಯ}} \emph{aidaneya} — fifth
\end{itemize}

Say \emph{aidu} and hold the first part. Your mouth does not stay still: it starts low and slides up toward \emph{i}. \textbf{Two sounds in one movement}, which is what the romanization's two letters are trying to show — and Kannada spends a single character on the whole slide.

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಐ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} turn clockwise through the compact left spiral and around its lower bowl
  \item \textbf{2.} without lifting, sweep through the join and around the broad right loop
  \item \textbf{3.} without lifting, carry the high arch leftward and finish at the open upper-left terminal
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 0.} Three movements rather than the four the others took, and all of them in one run: the left spiral and bowl flow through the broad right loop before the high arch finishes at the open upper-left terminal.

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — Kannada handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Gopala Krishna A, 'Kannada-alphabet-ai.gif', 28 frames, Wikimedia Commons, 25 May 2016, CC BY-SA 4.0.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two words and find \kn{ಐ} at the front of each
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಐದು}  ·  \kn{ಐದನೆಯ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಐ} three times without letting the pen leave the page
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ondu} and \emph{aidu}, and say which opening moves and which holds still
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಐ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ai}}.) Which number opens on it? (\textbf{\kn{ಐದು}}.) Does your mouth hold one position for it or two? (\textbf{Two} — it slides.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[r̥]{\kn{ಋ} — the vowel that sounds like a consonant}

\label{lesson:KA-S160-letter-vocalic-r}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಐ} — what sound, and how many movements?

Today's is the last of this chapter's six, and the one your pen works hardest for.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಋ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಋ}} — \emph{r̥}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — the shape \emph{r̥} takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside one.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಋತು}} \emph{r̥tu} — season, from the seasons chapter
\end{itemize}

\textbf{A vowel that sounds like an \emph{r} is a strange thing to be told}, and it is the honest description. This vowel came into Kannada with Sanskrit vocabulary, and it behaves like a vowel — it can hold a syllable on its own — while sounding close to the \emph{r} you already make. Telugu writes \te{ఋ} for the same sound, in the same borrowed words; so does Hindi, with \dv{ऋ}.

It is rare, and that is the reason it goes last rather than the reason to skip it: a rare shape inside a word you already know is exactly where a reader cannot tell whether the word or the printing is at fault.

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಋ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} turn clockwise around the compact upper-left spiral, descend through the outer curve, curl around the lower-left spiral, and sweep through the join around the rounded middle bowl
  \item \textbf{2.} lift, draw the inward bar from left to right, then curl upward into the high hook
  \item \textbf{3.} lift, sweep rightward around the lower bowl, climb its outer side, and finish at the open upper terminal
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2} — more than any other character in this chapter. Three pen-down runs: the double-spiral left body continues through the rounded middle bowl, then the high inward hook and the open right bowl are added separately.

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — Kannada handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Gopala Krishna A, 'Kannada-alphabet-ru.gif', 59 frames, Wikimedia Commons, 25 May 2016, CC BY-SA 4.0.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at the word below and find \kn{ಋ} at its front
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಋತು}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಋ} three times, counting the two lifts as you go
  \item \emph{Say it:} which of this chapter's characters took no lift at all
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಋ}? Is it a vowel or a consonant? (\textbf{A vowel} — it holds a syllable on its own, however close it sounds to \emph{r}.) How many times does your pen leave the page? (\textbf{Twice}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[svaragalu]{(\kn{ಆ} \kn{ಎ} \kn{ಏ} \kn{ಒ} \kn{ಐ} \kn{ಋ}) — six letters, sorted by the pen}

\label{lesson:KA-R78-vowels-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Count from one to ten in Kannada, and name the two characters that open numbers in that list.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script: the six, sorted by what the pen does}
\begin{quote}
\kn{ಆ} · \kn{ಎ} · \kn{ಏ} · \kn{ಒ} · \kn{ಐ} · \kn{ಋ}
\end{quote}

Sorting them by sound gives you a list to memorise. Sorting them by \textbf{what your hand does} gives you something to check yourself against:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{pen lifts} & \textbf{characters} & \textbf{what that means} \\
\midrule
none & \kn{ಎ} · \kn{ಒ} · \kn{ಐ} & one run, start to finish \\
one & \kn{ಆ} · \kn{ಏ} & a body, then one added piece \\
two & \kn{ಋ} & three separate runs \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Every one of these is attested rather than invented.} Each lesson printed the animation it came from, frame count and all, because a stroke order nobody published is a stroke order this book will not teach. The characters still waiting on a source keep the older instruction — copy what you see — and will until one turns up.

Five of the six open a word you can already say:

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಆರು} · \kn{ಎರಡು} · \kn{ಏಳು} · \kn{ಒಂದು} · \kn{ಐದು}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at the five words above and name the vowel each one opens on
  \item \emph{Say it:} which two of the six are a short and long pair
  \item \emph{Say it:} which one starts with a counterclockwise turn
  \item \emph{Trace it:} each of the six once, counting its lifts out loud
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the six needs two lifts? (\textbf{\kn{ಋ}}.) Which three need none? (\textbf{\kn{ಎ}}, \textbf{\kn{ಒ}}, \textbf{\kn{ಐ}}.) Which one is the long partner of \kn{ಎ}? (\textbf{\kn{ಏ}}.) And what does this book do about a character whose stroke order nobody has published? (\textbf{Teaches it by copying, and says so}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
